questions_and_answers.question: What term is used for the basic, simple infinitive form?
Which of the following consists of a past participle plus the infinitive of haben?
Which prepositions are given as examples of those that introduce infinitive phrases with 'zu'?
Which verb may be followed by an infinitive phrase?
Infinitives without 'zu' occur with which types of verbs?

answers.answer: Auxiliary verbs such as dürfen, können, möchten, müssen, sollen, wollen, werden and lassen

questions_and_answers.question: Which sentence illustrates the causative use of 'lassen'?

answers.answer: Ich muss einen Film entwickeln lassen
Kann ich meinen Wagen hinter dem Haus hier stehen lassen?
Hast du zum Reparieren des Wasserhahns das richtige Werkzeug da?

questions_and_answers.question: In which example does 'lassen' mean simply 'leave'?

answers.answer: Kann ich meinen Wagen hinter dem Haus hier stehen lassen?
Ich muss einen Film entwickeln lassen
Wir lernten Herrn und Frau Schulze kennen

questions_and_answers.question: How is the infinitive used as a noun in German?

answers.answer: It can function as a das-noun often equivalent to an English -ing form
It is always a verb prefix

questions_and_answers.question: Which example shows the infinitive used as a noun after a preposition meaning 'from'?

answers.answer: Wir lernten Herrn und Frau Schulze kennen
Das Auto blieb an der Ecke stehen

questions_and_answers.question: Which of the following verbs can be followed by an infinitive phrase?

articles.text:
C. INFINITIVES - SUMMARY AND REVIEW

The form of the infinitive was first noted in Unit 2, and subsequent discussion has referred only to the basic, simple infinitive form, also called the present infinitive. Both the perfect phrase and the passive phrase have infinitive forms, however, which can be referred to as perfect infinitives and passive infinitives. They consist of a past participle plus the infinitive form of the auxiliaries haben, sein or werden.

Here is a summary of infinitive forms:
Present infinitive (zu) kaufen — (to) buy
Perfect infinitive gekauft (zu) haben — (to) have bought
Passive infinitive gekauft (zu) werden — (to) be bought
Present infinitive (zu) gehen — (to) go
Perfect infinitive gegangen (zu) sein — (to) have gone

II. Infinitives occur with zu in infinitive phrases, and without zu in certain verb phrases.

1. Infinitive phrases with zu are introduced by prepositions, such as ohne and um: Ich gehe nicht gern fort, ohne etwas gegessen zu haben. They also occur after a great number of verbs in German: Ich habe dagegen nichts einzuwenden. Wir brauchen bloss über die Strasse zu gehen. Some of the most common verbs we have encountered, which may be followed by infinitive phrases, are: anfangen, beabsichtigen, beginnen, bitten, brauchen, haben, helfen, hoffen, sein, vergessen, versuchen, vorhaben.

2. Infinitives without zu occur in verb phrases with the auxiliary verbs dürfen, können, möchten, müssen, sollen, wollen, werden and lassen. Der Buchhändler wird Sie gern beraten. Ich habe mir überlegt, welches Wörterbuch ich kaufen sollte. Wir können uns verschiedene Apparate vorführen lassen. They may also occur in phrases with the verbs bleiben, hören, lernen and sehen: Die Ruine soll als Mahnmal stehen bleiben. Das Auto blieb an der Ecke stehen. Ich höre ihn im Badezimmer singen. Wir lernten Herrn und Frau Schulze in Deutschland kennen. Sehen Sie den Handwerker dort vor dem Haus stehen? You will note that this use of the infinitive in German often corresponds to the use of a verb form in -ing in English.

3. The verb lassen occurs with two different meanings in phrases with an infinitive. (1) Ich muss einen Film entwickeln lassen. (2) Kann ich meinen Wagen hinter dem Haus hier stehen lassen? The first example shows the use of lassen in a causative sense, meaning, that is, to have or get something done or to get or make someone do something. The infinitive with lassen in this construction is often equivalent to a past participle in English. The meaning of lassen in the second example is simply leave. Here the infinitive with lassen corresponds to an English verb form in -ing. Note too that in both languages this form may be omitted. Lassen is then the complete verb, not an auxiliary. Examples: Lass' das Bild an der Wand (hängen). Er lässt seine Bücher immer auf dem Tisch (liegen). Er hat seine Bücher auf dem Tisch liegen lassen. Er hat seine Bücher auf dem Tisch gelassen.

III. In Unit 11 we pointed out how the infinitive may be used as a das-noun in German, often equivalent to an English verb or noun form in -ing. The infinitive as a das-noun occurs frequently after prepositions. Ich komme gerade vom Schwimmen. (‘I've just come from a swim / from swimming.’) The use of the infinitive as a noun in this construction in German is equivalent sometimes to an English verb or noun form in -ing, sometimes to a different noun, sometimes to an infinitive and sometimes to a clause in English. Note the following examples:
Ich möchte beim Lesen nicht gestört werden. — I don't wish to be disturbed while I'm reading.
Sie ist beim Essen. — She's in the process of eating.
Hast du zum Reparieren des Wasserhahns das richtige Werkzeug da? — Do you have the right tools there to fix the water faucet?
Mit dem Entwickeln des Filmes hatte ich kein Glück. — I had no luck in developing the film.
Nach dem Lösen der Fahrkarte brachte ich meinen Koffer zur Gepäckaufgabe. — After getting my ticket I took my suitcase to the baggage room.
Während des Auspackens brachte der Page einen Brief. — While we were unpacking the bellhop brought a letter.
Durch das viele Waschen gingen die Hemden kaputt. — As a result of all the washing the shirts wore out.
